Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Calcium-driven regulation of voltage-sensing domains in BK channels" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Richard Aldrich (Senior Editor), a Reviewing Editor, and three reviewers.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

Details regarding the remaining concerns were initially developed in the comments from reviewer #1, but all reviewers were in agreement that, if these concerns are addressed, it will greatly improve the paper and provide a better framework for evaluating the implications of the present work without the context of earlier work. As a general comment, several of the arguments developed in the responses to the initial reviews would be useful in clarifying for readers what was done in this paper, and the rationale for various inferences (point 4 below). In particular, both figures that were included in the response to reviewers would be valuable additions as supplementary figures. Similarly, although the new manuscript includes the analysis from the two-high-affinity binding site model in Table 1, readers may find it odd that fits from these models are not included on main figures (or at least in figure supplements) in the paper. In particular, as reviewer #1 notes, although Table 1 supports the view that Model II does better than Model I, even for the two Ca site formulation, visually comparing these in fits to the Q-V and VH-Ca curves would give us a better feel for how well the data may discriminate between Model I and Model II (point 2 below). We therefore recommend including comparisons of fits on relevant panels, either in the main figures or, if that seems too cluttered, perhaps in supplementary figures.

There are four main categories of concern/recommendations corresponding to the itemization of reviewer #1.

1) Although the new information regarding gating current decay time constants is a valuable addition to the paper, there are aspects of this data that maintain the concern that Ca-equilibration with subunits with active voltage sensors may impact on the gating current decay time course, particularly at intermediate Ca. In particularly, the separation of calculated Ca equilibration rates and the observed time constants may not be as distinct as one might like. This might potentially impact the steepness of the VH-Ca relationship. I would recommend that the figure included in the rebuttal that plots the z∂ and residuals as a function of ratio of τCa binding/τgating currents be made into a supplementary figure, but with the addition that the analysis be done both using the first 30 μs and also the first 100 μs for comparison. Reviewer #1 also includes an additional suggestion for such a figure. Please also check whether the discontinuity in the plot of residuals observed at τ ratios of about 4 and 5 is a feature of the simulation or something else. Such a discontinuity seems a bit odd for a simulated data.

Also pertinent to this issue, two reviewers point out that the example gating current decay time constants from the new Figure 1A and 1B may not be fully consistent with the averaged data in Figure 1C. E.g., the time constant in 1B is above 0.8 of that in 1A, while at +160 mV in 1C, the time constants at 100 μM are about 0.5 that at 0 μM.

2) Showing the fits to the two Ca binding site formulation needs to be included, as mentioned above. Even if Model I and Model II give fits that extensively overlap, it is useful to know this. Similarly, a comparison of how much different the fits are with single site and two site Ca binding formulations would be helpful.

3) There appear to be some discrepancies in the properties of OFF gating current time constants that need to be addressed.

4) As stated at the outset, there is information in the response to reviewers that should be included in the manuscript to help guide readers.

Overall, all of these issues can presumably be addressed without new experiments. We hope the authors will agree that these recommendations will strengthen an interesting paper and better help the intended audience place this work within the context of previous work on BK channel gating.

Reviewer #1:

The authors' response and modifications to the manuscript are helpful and address many of my questions. However, there are still some issues that require clarification.

1) Appendix, subsection “Assumptions and model predictions”, third paragraph: "Ca2+ binding at this Ca2+ concentration proceeds at a pace about 33-fold slower than the voltage sensor movement (~30 μs)."

The new kinetic data (Figure 1C) indicates that the gating current time constant is actually as slow as 75 μs near VH (i.e. slower than 0 Ca). That, and the simulated effect of Ca-binding kinetics in response to my previous review, have increased concerns about the assumption that Ca binding does not re-equilibrate during gating current measurements at intermediate [Ca], and I think this issue requires some additional analysis. This assumption is critical for modeling the Ca-dependence of the Q-V data and distinguishing between Schemes I and II. The simulation indicates that if Ca binding can re-equilibrate, then Q-Vs predicted by Scheme I will become more Boltzmann-like, potentially making it more difficult to distinguish Schemes I and II. In addition, I wonder if re-equilibration could contribute to the remarkable steepness of the VH-Ca relation between 5 and 10 μm Ca – a feature that is not well described by any of the models. That is, re-equilibration should increase the VH shift (since voltage-sensor activation will enhance Ca-binding) and if Ca re-equilibration is faster at higher [Ca] then it would tend to increase the steepness of the curve

The 75 μs gating current time constant in Figure 1C increases my concern because it is potentially closer to the time constant of Ca binding. For example, at the [Ca] used in the simulation (15 μM), the on-rate at a single binding site would be 1500 s-1, or 6000 s-1 for the transition from zero to one Ca bound with 4 binding sites, implying a time constant less than 166 μs (depending on off-rate). Thus, it seems possible that Ca-binding could be only ~2 fold slower than voltage sensor activation under some conditions. The simulation seems to suggest this is probably not a problem since there is little change in the Q-V fit parameters when the Ca-binding time constant is 3-fold or more slower than gating current. However, I have two concerns about the simulation analysis: (1) the Q-Vs were measured by fitting the first 30 μs of the simulated gating current, whereas the experimental data were measured from the first 100 μs. This could lead the simulation to underestimate the potential contribution of Ca re-equilibration to the data. (2) It doesn't seem reasonable to fit the simulated Q-Vs with a single Boltzmann function if the assumption to be tested (no re-equilibration) predicts a double-Boltzmann Q-V. In other words, although the simulation shows little change in the Q-V fit parameters when the Ca-binding time constant is 3-fold or more slower than gating current, I wonder if this indicates that there is no change in the Q-V over this range, or merely that the fits to a single Boltzmann function are all equally bad. I think the simulation analysis should be repeated by fitting the initial 100 μs of the gating current, and fitting the resulting Q-Vs to the prediction when there is no re-equilibration of Ca (i.e. double Boltzmann). Presumably, such fits, or showing the actual Q-Vs, would better define the conditions under which the model assumptions are valid. Plotting VH might also be useful.

2) Although I accept the conclusion, based on Table 1, that Scheme II fits the data better than Scheme I even with 2 binding sites per subunit, I think it would be good to show the fits for the 2-site models, at least in the supplement. One reason, as I suggested in my initial review, is that I don't think it is reasonable to dismiss Scheme I based on the qualitative difference in Q-V shape for a one-site model, when such a model is model is inconsistent with the data in Figure 5. That is simply a "straw man" argument. But, mainly, as noted by another reviewer, none of the models fit very well, suggesting neither Schemes are the final answer. In such a situation, I think it is important to show the fits for future reference.

3) The authors partially addressed my question about gating current kinetics with Figure 1C. The time constants for the ON currents do appear to shift along the voltage-axis in response to Ca, consistent with the Q-V. But they didn't address my question regarding the relatively small 2.5-fold Ca-dependent change in OFF kinetics in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The authors suggest, based on Figure 1C that the main effect Ca is to slow OFF kinetics, but Figure 2—figure supplement 1 isn't consistent with that prediction. Presumably if ON time constants are decreased ~2-fold by Ca then OFF time constants should increase ~10 fold to account for the large E-factor. Are the data representative? Can OFF kinetics included in the time constant plot?

4) Finally, many of the responses to reviewers are fine, but should be incorporated in the manuscript. Requests for clarification generally refer to issues that need to be better explained not only to the reviewers but also to the intended audience of the paper. For example, when I requested clarification in the Materials and methods section regarding the grounding scheme, I meant that such details should be included in the Materials and methods section. Similarly, the author's clarification that representative traces in Figure 2A are from different patches with the exception of 0 and 100 Ca is helpful, but should be described in the figure legend.

The revised manuscript is improved and adequately addresses most of my concerns. However, the authors expressed some confusion over my questions regarding the apparent discrepancy in OFF gating current kinetics, which I will attempt to clarify.

"We are somewhat confused about the reviewer 1 comment 3. As stated in Results the 𝜏𝐺−𝑂𝑁(𝑉) curves were fitted to a two-state model (𝜏(𝑉)=1/(𝛼(𝑉)+𝛽(𝑉)) where the forward (𝛼) and backward (𝛽) rate constants represent the resting-active (R-A) transitions of the voltage sensors determining the equilibrium constant of the VSD activation (𝐽(𝑉)=𝛼(𝑉)𝛽(𝑉)). My questions about gating current kinetics (Comments #3 in previous review, #1 in original review) relate in large part to the data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. I asked whether the difference in gating current kinetics shown for 0 and 10 μm Ca in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 are consistent with a large Q-V shift (as observed in 10 Ca). The fast OFF component at -90 mV should be a relatively direct measure of the backward rate β (i.e. τ~=1/β). If there is a small change in ON kinetics and large Q-V shift, then there should be a large change in β and hence OFF kinetics. The authors make essentially the same prediction based on their fits to the ON kinetics in Figure 1C. But they do not include OFF data to directly confirm the prediction or address my concern.

I do not think that measurements of OFF kinetics at multiple voltages are necessary. Measurements at a single voltage like -90 mV should suffice. Based on Figure 2—figure supplement 1, such data already exists.

results.result: BK channels are modular proteins regulated by both cytosolic Ca2+ and voltage, with distinct structural domains (VSD, CTD with RCK1/RCK2) that independently modulate channel gating. In the absence of Ca2+, very positive voltages are required for channel activation, making Ca2+ sensor activation necessary for physiological function.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C10 are all supported by extensive citations to prior literature and represent well-established background knowledge about BK channel structure and function. These claims provide the foundational context for the study and are not contested.

results.result: Prior work suggests energetic interactions between voltage and Ca2+ sensors are important for BK channel activation, with the CTD-VSD interface mediating crosstalk. However, the strength and mechanism of this interaction remain debated, and the RCK1 site has been specifically implicated in communicating Ca2+-dependent changes to the VSD.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C19 accurately summarize the state of prior knowledge and open questions in the field, all supported by appropriate citations. These claims establish the motivation for the current study by identifying gaps in understanding.

results.result: The study's main findings are that Ca2+ sensor occupancy strongly impacts VSD activation through a coordinated mechanism where Ca2+ binding to a single α-subunit affects all VSDs equally, with RCK1 and RCK2 sites contributing equally to decrease the free energy for VSD activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22 represent the primary conclusions of the study and are supported by the experimental data from gating current measurements and mutational analysis presented in the Results section. The coordinated interaction mechanism is validated through model fitting (C78), and the equal contribution of RCK1 and RCK2 is demonstrated through mutant analysis (C88, C89, C91).

results.result: The fast IG-ON relaxation reflects voltage sensor movement in the closed channel conformation, occurring before channel opening, as demonstrated by kinetic analysis showing the gating current decays before ionic current activation reaches exponential time course.
results.evaluation: Claims C23, C24, and C26 are directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B. The temporal separation between gating current decay and ionic current activation provides clear evidence that the measured gating currents reflect closed-state voltage sensor movements.

results.result: OFF-gating currents show Ca2+-dependent changes in amplitude and kinetics, with at least two resolvable components. The fast component time constants agree with two-state model predictions, while the slow component increases with Ca2+ concentration, reflecting increased channel open probability.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C39 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2 and supplementary figures. The kinetic analysis and model fitting provide consistent evidence for the interpretation of the OFF-gating current components.

results.result: The standard Horrigan-Aldrich model assumes a single Ca2+-binding site per subunit and independent CTD-VSD interaction (Scheme I). At extreme Ca2+ concentrations, VSD activation is mechanism-independent, but at intermediate concentrations, Scheme II (concerted interaction) predicts distinct behavior characterized by a five-component Boltzmann function. Ca2+-binding is slow enough to ignore re-equilibration during gating current measurements.
results.evaluation: Claims C41, C44, C46, and C49 describe the theoretical framework and modeling assumptions. C41 accurately describes the HA model based on citations. C44 and C46 are logical inferences from the model structure. C49 is supported by kinetic simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, demonstrating that fast Ca2+ re-equilibration cannot explain the data.

results.result: Model II (Scheme II), where Ca2+ binding to one subunit affects all VSDs equally, reproduces the Ca2+-dependent gating charge movement better than Model I (independent subunit interaction).
results.evaluation: Claim C78 is supported by the model fitting results shown in Figure 4B-D and Table 1. The Akaike Information Criterion analysis strongly favors Model II (wi = 0.004 for one-site model, wi = 0.995 for two-site Model II), providing quantitative support for the concerted interaction mechanism.

results.result: Mutations in RCK1 (D362A/D367A and M513I) and RCK2 (5D5A) sites show that both high-affinity Ca2+-binding sites contribute approximately equally (~4 kJ/mol each) to decreasing the free energy for VSD activation, suggesting independent allosteric pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C56, C58, C61, and C64 are supported by experimental data from mutant analysis shown in Figures 5 and 6. The similar energetic contributions (ΔΔG ~4 kJ/mol) from disrupting either RCK1 or RCK2 sites provide strong evidence for equal and additive effects, supporting independent pathways.

results.result: Selective disruption of RCK1 (D362A/D367A) or RCK2 (5D5A) Ca2+-binding sites by neutralizing coordinating residues reveals that both sites contribute equally (~4 kJ/mol) to VSD activation, and their combined effect mimics full Ca2+ occupancy.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 and C91 are directly supported by the mutant gating current data in Figure 5. The experimental measurements show nearly identical energetic contributions from each site, and the additive nature of the effects supports the conclusion of independent contributions.

results.result: Fluorescence studies show that Ca2+-binding causes VSD rearrangements and voltage-dependent gating ring reorganization. These conformational changes are attributable to VSD operation rather than pore opening, as mutations affecting pore equilibrium do not alter voltage-dependent gating ring reorganization.
results.evaluation: Claims C72, C73, and C75 are supported by citations to prior fluorescence studies (Savalli et al., 2012; Miranda et al., 2013, 2018). These claims accurately represent findings from the cited literature and provide important context for interpreting the current results.

results.result: The concerted CTD-VSD communication may be analogous to the mechanism in bacterial K+ channels (MthK), where Ca2+-binding triggers symmetric gating ring rearrangement propagated to transmembrane domains. Each Ca2+-binding event may produce gradual gating ring expansion affecting all four voltage sensors through protein-protein interfaces.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 are explicitly speculative (C81 states "we can speculate"). While C80 is supported by citations to structural studies, the analogy to bacterial channels and the proposed gradual expansion mechanism remain hypothetical. The speculation is reasonable but lacks direct experimental validation in this study.

results.result: The CTD-VSD communication pathway involves non-covalent interactions between the RCK1 N-lobe and S0-S4 transmembrane segments. Ca2+-binding causes the RCK1 N-lobe to pull on S6 and modify contact surfaces with adjacent voltage sensors. Prior work suggested RCK1 is primarily responsible for CTD-VSD coupling.
results.evaluation: Claims C82, C84, C85, and C86 are supported by citations to structural and functional studies. However, the current study's findings (C89, C91) challenge the prior view that RCK1 is primarily responsible, showing instead that RCK2 contributes equally. This represents an important advance over prior understanding.

results.result: The two RCK sensors appear to contribute independently to VSD modulation, though modest cooperativity between them cannot be ruled out. Prior studies suggest intrasubunit cooperativity is more relevant than intersubunit cooperativity, but the current study's cooperativity analysis produced results inconsistent with previous reports.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C99 present a mixed picture. The independence of RCK1 and RCK2 contributions is supported by the additive effects (C88, C91). However, C98 notes that including cooperativity in the model produces results "at odds with previous reports," and the model fitting with cooperativity yields unrealistic KD values (Table 1). The cooperativity question remains unresolved.

results.result: While Model II (concerted CTD-VSD interaction) better explains the data than Model I (independent interaction), more work is needed to develop improved models that more accurately reproduce CTD-VSD interaction properties.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 is a reasonable concluding statement acknowledging the study's limitations. The AIC analysis clearly favors Model II, but the authors appropriately note that neither model perfectly captures all aspects of the mechanism, particularly regarding cooperativity between Ca2+ sites.

results.result: The study used human BK α-subunit and mutants expressed in Xenopus oocytes, with recordings made using inside-out patch-clamp. Gating currents were elicited by 1 ms voltage steps from -90 to 350 mV.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C105 are straightforward methodological details that are adequately described. The methods are standard for this type of study and appear appropriate for measuring gating currents.

results.result: The authors report that Ca²⁺ sensor occupancy has a strong impact on VSD activation through a coordinated mechanism where Ca²⁺ binding to a single α-subunit affects all VSDs equally, and that both RCK1 and RCK2 Ca²⁺-binding sites contribute equally to decreasing the free energy necessary to activate the VSD. This leads to the conclusion that voltage-dependent gating and pore opening in BK channels is modulated to a great extent by the interaction between Ca²⁺ sensors and VSDs.
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge this as an important contribution, but raise substantive concerns about data analysis, methodology, and interpretation. Reviewer #1 notes the findings 'contradict previous studies making it more difficult to assess their significance' and requests additional kinetic analysis and clarification of how QC is determined. Reviewers express concern that 'none of the models fit very well' (Reviewer #2) and request more rigorous comparison with previous work by Horrigan and Aldrich. The editors state the results are 'currently difficult to interpret mechanistically' and that requested changes will 'place this work on a stronger foundation.'

results.result: The authors claim that the fast IG-ON relaxation exhibits almost complete decay before IK achieves exponential time course in 0 Ca²⁺ conditions, with a time constant of ~3.4 ms at 160 mV, and that this fast IG-ON relaxation reflects movement of gating charge in the channel's closed conformation regardless of internal Ca²⁺ concentration.
results.evaluation: Reviewer #2 specifically requests that 'this statement could be supported by showing ionic currents along with gating currents at the same voltages. The comparison in high [Ca] (≥10 µM) would be particularly helpful.' Reviewer #1 extensively questions whether QC measurements might be contaminated by later voltage sensor movements and requests 'examples of the time course of current activation under identical conditions of higher Ca²⁺ to provide assurance that QC is not being affected by channel opening.' The editors emphasize these concerns need elaboration.

results.result: The authors report that OFF-gating current was dramatically modified with smaller amplitude and slower kinetics as internal Ca²⁺ increased, with at least two components (fast and slow) resolved in the decay, and that the relative contribution of the slower component increases with Ca²⁺, reflecting increased open probability.
results.evaluation: Reviewer #1 raises concerns about apparent discrepancies in OFF gating current kinetics, noting 'a relatively small 2.5-fold Ca-dependent change in OFF kinetics in Figure 2—figure supplement 1' which 'doesn't seem compatible with a large Q-V shift.' The reviewer asks 'How can these effects be reconciled with the proposed 26-fold change in equilibrium constant?' and requests that 'OFF kinetics be included in the time constant plot.' In subsequent reviews, this concern persists with Reviewer #1 stating the data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 'isn't consistent with that prediction.'

results.result: The authors claim that Scheme II (concerted CTD-VSD interaction model) reproduces reasonably well the behavior of Ca²⁺-dependent gating charge movement observed in their experiments.
results.evaluation: Reviewer #1 challenges the adequacy of model testing, stating 'I don't think this is an adequate test of the two mechanisms' because 'both models incorporate a single Ca site per subunit, inconsistent with the conclusion from Figure 4 that both sites contribute equally to voltage sensor activation.' The reviewer requests analysis of whether 'the data can discriminate between versions of Schemes I and II with two binding sites per subunit.' Reviewer #2 notes 'neither model fits the data well (Figure 3).' The editors emphasize that 'the conclusions from the considerations in Figure 2 and 3 seem less strongly based than one would like.'

results.result: The authors report that both high-affinity Ca²⁺-binding sites (RCK1 and RCK2) contribute approximately equally to the decrease in free energy necessary to activate the VSD, with the energetic effect being practically identical (~−4 kJ/mol) for both D362A/D367A and 5D5A mutations, establishing that RCK2-driven contribution to CTD-VSD energetic coupling is quite similar to RCK1-driven contribution.
results.evaluation: Reviewer #3 states the authors 'present compelling evidence that Ca-binding to the cytosolic domain does allosterically influence VSD equilibrium and, furthermore, that each of the two Ca binding sites on a single BK α subunit independently, and largely additively, influence the VSD equilibrium.' While reviewers request additional analysis and clarification of methods, none directly challenge these mutant-based findings. The equal contribution of both sites is accepted as a key finding.

results.result: The authors report that both D362A/D367A and M513I mutations affect Ca²⁺-induced enhancement of VSD activation very similarly through the RCK1 site, revealing an additive effect of Ca²⁺-binding to RCK1 and Ca²⁺ bowl sites on VSD activation, suggesting independent allosteric pathways, though the authors acknowledge they cannot eliminate the possibility of some cooperativity.
results.evaluation: Reviewer #3 explicitly notes the authors 'reveal that occupancy of any binding site allosterically influences the VSD equilibrium of all subunits' and that the sites act 'independently, and largely additively.' While Reviewer #1 raises questions about cooperativity in modeling, the experimental findings from the mutants regarding independent contributions are not directly challenged. The data supporting independent pathways is accepted.

results.result: The authors claim that Ca²⁺-binding is slow enough to safely ignore calcium re-equilibration during the 100 μs it takes to measure the gating charges.
results.evaluation: Reviewer #1 expresses substantial concern about this assumption, stating 'I have some concern that it might not be' valid. The reviewer notes 'Ca-equilibration may only be ~4-5 slower than voltage-sensor movement. Is that enough of a difference?' In subsequent reviews, Reviewer #1 states 'the new kinetic data (Figure 1C) indicates that the gating current time constant is actually as slow as 75 μs near VH' which 'increased concerns about the assumption that Ca binding does not re-equilibrate during gating current measurements at intermediate [Ca].' The reviewer requests additional simulation analysis to validate this critical assumption.

results.result: The authors describe assumptions of the Horrigan-Aldrich model and propose that at extreme Ca²⁺ conditions VSD activation behaves in a mechanism-independent manner, while the Ca²⁺-binding effect on VSD activation according to Scheme II is characterized by a five-component Boltzmann function.
results.evaluation: These are primarily methodological and theoretical framework claims that reviewers do not directly challenge. Reviewer #1 requests clarification of model assumptions and testing, but does not dispute the mathematical framework itself. The description of model assumptions and predictions is accepted as accurate representation of the theoretical approaches.

results.result: The authors discuss the structural and mechanistic basis for CTD-VSD coupling, citing evidence that functional activation of the gating ring is propagated to the VSD, that gating ring rearrangement has voltage dependence attributable to voltage sensor operation, and that the communication pathway involves non-covalent interactions between RCK1 N-lobe and S0-S4 transmembrane segments, with selective activation of RCK1 domain being responsible for Ca²⁺-induced VSD rearrangement.
results.evaluation: These claims are primarily based on citations to published structural and functional studies. Reviewer #2 notes 'there is also no evidence to distinguish if such an allosteric mechanism for Ca²⁺ binding to affect VSD activation is mediated by the covalent pulling of the C-linker or non-covalent interaction' and states 'the present data seems not sufficient to exclude the contribution by the other mechanism.' However, reviewers do not challenge the authors' interpretation of published structural data. The discussion is accepted as reasonable interpretation of existing literature.

results.result: The authors speculate that the concerted CTD-VSD communication may underlie a mechanism analogous to bacterial K⁺ channels, where Ca²⁺-site occupancy triggers symmetric rearrangement of the cytosolic tetrameric structure, and that each Ca²⁺-binding event produces gradual conformational expansion of the gating ring affecting all four voltage sensors.
results.evaluation: These are explicitly speculative claims drawing analogies to bacterial channels. Reviewers do not challenge these speculations as inappropriate. Reviewer #3 notes the authors 'undertake an analysis of a potential mechanism' and the speculation is accepted as reasonable discussion of potential mechanisms based on structural analogies.

results.result: The authors discuss cooperativity between Ca²⁺-binding sites, citing evidence for modest cooperativity, structural connectivity supporting cooperative interactions, and functional studies suggesting intrasubunit cooperativity is more relevant than intersubunit cooperativity, while acknowledging that their analysis with cooperativity produced results at odds with previous reports and that more work is required to explore improved models.
results.evaluation: These claims primarily cite published literature and acknowledge limitations of the current study. Reviewer #1 requests analysis of cooperativity in modeling, but the authors' discussion of cooperativity based on literature and their acknowledgment of model limitations is not challenged. The balanced discussion of cooperativity and model limitations is accepted.

results.result: The authors provide background on BK channel structure and function, including regulation by Ca²⁺ and voltage, tetrameric structure with VSD and CTD domains, RCK domains with Ca²⁺-binding sites, allosteric gating mechanisms, and structural information from Aplysia BK channel revealing CTD-VSD interfaces.
results.evaluation: These are background claims supported by extensive citations to published literature. Reviewers do not challenge these established facts about BK channel structure and function. This background information is accepted as accurate representation of the field.

results.result: The authors describe the properties of mutants used in the study, including that M513I eliminates Ca²⁺ sensitivity mediated by the RCK1 site, and that D362A/D367A and 5D5A selectively impair Ca²⁺-sensitivity of RCK1 and RCK2 sensors respectively by neutralizing residues involved in Ca²⁺-coordination.
results.evaluation: These claims describe established properties of mutants from published studies. Reviewers do not challenge the characterization of these mutants. The description of mutant properties is accepted based on cited literature.

results.result: The authors describe methodological details including the source of cDNA constructs, use of Xenopus oocytes as expression system, patch-clamp recording technique in inside-out configuration, and voltage step protocols for gating current measurements.
results.evaluation: These are standard methodological details. While reviewers request clarification of some methodological aspects (e.g., grounding scheme, time between test steps), they do not challenge the basic methods described. The methodological approach is accepted as appropriate.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the primary conclusions (C20-C22). OpenEval finds them SUPPORTED by experimental data and model fitting. Peer reviewers rate them UNCERTAIN, acknowledging importance but raising substantive concerns about data analysis, model fitting quality, and contradictions with previous studies. Major disagreement on confidence level.

Both evaluate claims about gating current measurements reflecting closed-state voltage sensor movements (C23, C24, C26). OpenEval finds them SUPPORTED by Figure 1A-B data. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting additional ionic current comparisons at same voltages and expressing concern about potential contamination from later voltage sensor movements. Disagreement on sufficiency of evidence.

Both evaluate OFF-gating current kinetics claims (C34-C39). OpenEval finds them SUPPORTED by Figure 2 data and kinetic analysis. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting apparent discrepancies between small 2.5-fold Ca-dependent change in OFF kinetics versus large Q-V shift, questioning how effects reconcile with proposed 26-fold equilibrium constant change. Significant disagreement on internal consistency.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, challenging adequacy of model testing since both models use single Ca site per subunit inconsistent with two-site conclusion, and noting neither model fits data well. Major disagreement on model validation.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, expressing substantial concern that Ca-equilibration may only be 4-5x slower than voltage sensor movement and requesting additional simulation analysis. Disagreement on validity of critical assumption.
